Translation degrees in the UK and Ireland: where to study

June 12, 2019
Education | Careers | Professional Translation

Choosing where to study translation is a big decision, because the course you pick shapes the languages, specialisms and contacts you leave with. The UK and Ireland offer a wide range of translation degrees, from undergraduate programmes to specialist master's courses that train you for professional practice.

This list covers translation degrees and master's programmes at universities in England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. Course titles, language pairs and entry requirements change each year, so check the official course page before you apply.

What a translation degree involves

A translation degree combines advanced language work with translation theory and practical projects. Most courses now include computer-assisted translation tools, terminology management and project management, because that is how professional translators work today.

Some programmes also teach interpreting, subtitling or localisation. If you want to work in a particular field, such as legal, medical or technical translation, look for courses that offer specialist modules or industry placements.

Undergraduate translation degrees

Few UK universities offer a degree focused only on translation at undergraduate level. Most students take a modern languages degree, with translation as a module or a final-year specialism, and move on to a master's in translation afterwards.

If you want translation from the first year, these are two programmes to look at:

  • Cardiff University offers a BA in Translation, with a variant that includes a placement year abroad.
  • London Metropolitan University lists a BA (Hons) in Translation.

Many other universities offer modern languages degrees. Compare the module lists on each course page to see whether translation is taught and how much of it you will actually study.

Postgraduate translation degrees in England

England has the largest choice of master's courses in translation. These programmes are among the best known:

  • University of Leeds, MA Applied Translation Studies, a technology-focused course covering computer-assisted translation, machine translation, localisation and project management.
  • Newcastle University, MA Translation and Interpreting, with Translation Studies and other related MAs also listed by the university.
  • University of Westminster, MA Translation and Interpreting, based in central London with training in translation, conference interpreting and public service interpreting.
  • Durham University, MA Translation Studies, available full time or part time.
  • University of Manchester, MA Translation and Interpreting Studies, open to any language combination with English.
  • University of Surrey, MA Translation, one of the longest-running translation programmes in the world.

Other universities, including the University of Bristol, offer research degrees in translation studies, which suit you if you want an academic career.

Postgraduate translation degrees in Scotland

Scotland has two strong options for postgraduate study:

  • Heriot-Watt University, MSc Interpreting and Translating, a one-year course in Edinburgh that pairs English with one or two of Spanish, German, Chinese or French. Heriot-Watt also runs a separate MSc in Interpreting.
  • University of Edinburgh, MSc Translation Studies, a one-year full-time or two-year part-time course where you work with two languages alongside English.

Postgraduate translation degrees in Wales

Wales offers translation courses at two universities:

  • Cardiff University, MA Translation Studies, which teaches theory and practice and allows you to specialise in areas such as legal, medical or scientific translation.
  • Swansea University, MA Professional Translation, alongside an MA in Translation and Interpreting with an extended two-year route.

Translation degrees in Northern Ireland

Northern Ireland has fewer options. Queen's University Belfast lists an MA in Translation covering audiovisual and literary translation, and a separate MA in Interpreting.

If you prefer to start with a broader degree, Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University both offer modern languages programmes that you can follow with a specialist master's elsewhere.

Translation degrees in the Republic of Ireland

Two Irish universities stand out for translation:

  • Dublin City University, MA Translation Studies, a one-year full-time course that belongs to the European Master's in Translation network and covers how AI tools are changing the profession.
  • Trinity College Dublin, MPhil in Literary Translation, where you build a portfolio of translations and balance theory with practice.

How to choose the right translation master's

Start with your language pair, because some courses only support certain combinations. Then check whether the course is a member of a professional or academic network, such as CIUTI or the European Master's in Translation network, and whether it includes work placements.

It also helps to think about your career goal. If you want to work in the language industry, a course with strong translation technology training will serve you well. If you want to work in the public sector, an interpreting-focused course may be a better fit.

Working as a translator after your degree

A degree is the first step. Most translators also build experience through freelance work, agency work or in-house roles, and many take professional exams run by bodies such as the Chartered Institute of Linguists.

BeTranslated works with professional translators and interpreters across many languages and sectors, and many of them began their careers on courses like these. If your business needs translation or remote interpreting, you can request a free quote.

Frequently asked questions

Which UK universities offer a degree in translation?

Cardiff University and London Metropolitan University list single honours translation degrees at undergraduate level. At master's level, universities including Leeds, Newcastle, Westminster, Durham, Manchester, Heriot-Watt, Edinburgh and Cardiff offer translation or translation and interpreting courses.

Do I need a degree to become a translator?

Translation is not a regulated profession in the UK, so no single qualification is compulsory. Many employers and agencies still look for a degree or professional qualification plus proven experience, and many translators specialise in one field.

What is the difference between translation and interpreting courses?

Translation courses train you to work with written text, while interpreting courses train you to work with the spoken word, in settings such as conferences, courts and hospitals. Some universities, such as Westminster and Heriot-Watt, teach both.

How long does a master's in translation take?

Most master's courses in translation take one year full time or two years part time. Some universities offer an extended two-year route that includes a period abroad.

Can I study translation if I only speak one foreign language?

Yes. Most master's programmes ask you to work between English and one other language, and some allow a second. Check the entry requirements on each course page, as universities set their own language standards.
